summary: Defines GMPLS signaling extensions for Shared Mesh Protection (SMP), where several working paths can share backup resources. It builds on ITU-T recommendations G.808.3 and G.873.3 and on the requirements in RFC 7412. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Several roads share one spare bridge. If one road fails, traffic uses the spare. This document teaches the network how to reserve and switch to that shared bridge.

subtitle: RSVP-TE signaling that lets several backup paths share resources and be switched on by a data-plane protocol.

tldr.problem: Shared Mesh Protection activates a backup path through a data-plane protocol rather than control-plane signaling, so nodes must be told during setup that a path uses this mode.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a "Shared Mesh Protection" LSP Protection Type to the PROTECTION object, adjusts the N and O bits, adds an 8-bit preemption priority, and defines two Notify error sub-codes for shared-resource availability.
tldr.outcome: Backup paths for disjoint working paths can pre-reserve shared resources, and the APS protocol activates one when a working path fails.

today: RFC 9270 is a Proposed Standard from August 2022 and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 4872 and RFC 4873.

sections.title: Why Shared Mesh Protection Needs Signaling
sections.content:
RFC 4872 defines RSVP-TE extensions for Shared Mesh Restoration (SMR), a kind of preplanned LSP rerouting where multiple protecting Label Switched Paths (LSPs) share link and node resources. RFC 4873 details the encoding of the last 32-bit Reserved field of the PROTECTION object.

Shared Mesh Protection (SMP) is defined generically by ITU-T G.808.3, with G.873.3 covering the ODU layer and RFC 7412 giving requirements for MPLS-TP. SMP differs from SMR in activation: SMP activates a protecting LSP through the Automatic Protection Switching (APS) protocol in the data plane when the working LSP fails, while SMR uses control-plane signaling. Nodes must know which mode is in use, and SMP has advantages in recovery speed.

RFC 9270 updates RFC 4872 and RFC 4873 with GMPLS signaling extensions. Only generic aspects are addressed; technology-specific aspects and management (YANG) are left to other documents.
sections.eli5: There are two ways to switch to the spare road: ask a central office, or let the road workers do it on the spot. This document is about telling everyone the second way is in use.

sections.title: What SMP Is
sections.content:
SMP is based on precomputed protecting LSPs that are preconfigured in the network elements. Preconfiguring means pre-reserving resources without activating a particular protecting LSP; for example, cross-connects in intermediate nodes of the protecting LSP are not preestablished.

Because protecting LSPs are not activated, link and node resources can be shared by the protecting LSPs of multiple working LSPs, which are disjoint and so unlikely to fail together. Protecting LSPs are activated on a working LSP failure or an operator command, using APS messages exchanged along the protecting LSP in the data plane. SMP is always revertive.
sections.eli5: Spare roads are planned ahead but left closed. Because the main roads are far apart, they rarely break together, so they can share the same spare.

sections.title: How a Protection Switch Happens
sections.content:
The RFC's example topology has working LSPs [A,B,C,D] and [H,I,J,K], protected by [A,E,F,G,D] and [H,E,F,G,K]. The protecting LSPs share resources along nodes E, F and G, such as link capacity and node cross-connects.

When a failure such as Signal Fail (SF) or Signal Degrade (SD) hits working LSP [A,B,C,D], end node A sends a switching request APS message to node E and waits for confirmation. If resources are available, E confirms to A and forwards the request to F. When A gets the confirmation it sets up its cross-connection and bridges traffic to the protecting LSP. E then waits for a confirmation from F before making its own cross-connection.

If the protection resource is unavailable, the intermediate node MUST notify the end node (see Section 5.5). If it is held by a lower-priority protecting LSP, that service is removed and the switch proceeds. If node E fails to allocate the resource it MUST notify A, and A stops bridging and selecting traffic.
sections.eli5: When a road breaks, the first town asks the next town along the spare road if it is free. Each town says yes in turn, and then cars start using the spare.

sections.title: Signaling the Primary and Secondary LSPs
sections.content:
The protected (primary working) LSP and the secondary (protecting) LSP belong to the same session, so the SESSION object MUST be the same, but the LSP ID MUST differ. The new type applies only to bidirectional LSPs.

The PROTECTION object goes in the Path message with LSP Protection Type "Shared Mesh Protection". Primary LSPs set S=0, P=0 and N=1, with the ASSOCIATION object holding the secondary LSP_ID. The N bit is set because protection switching is signaled in the data plane.

Secondary LSPs set S, P and N to 1, with the ASSOCIATION object holding the primary LSP_ID, which MUST be known beforehand. The Path message MUST include at least one PRIMARY_PATH_ROUTE object to allow resource sharing. Resources MUST be pre-reserved but not committed in the data plane. After switching, the protecting LSP MUST be signaled with S=0 and O=1 and its resources MUST be allocated. The formerly working LSP MAY be signaled with the A bit set in ADMIN_STATUS. Extra traffic is left for further study.
sections.eli5: Each road gets a ticket saying what kind of road it is and which road it backs up. The spare road's ticket says it is reserved but not yet in use.

sections.title: Updated PROTECTION Object Fields
sections.content:
A new LSP Protection Type flag 0x20 means Shared Mesh Protection. The rules in Section 14.2 of RFC 4872 ensure all nodes along an SMP LSP are SMP aware, so there are no backward-compatibility issues.

The Notification (N) bit now applies also to 0x20, and for SMP the N bit MUST be set to 1. The Operational (O) bit, which says the protecting LSP is carrying traffic after switching, now applies to 0x20 as well.

An 8-bit Preemption Priority field is allocated from formerly reserved bits. It is set by the network operator at the end nodes, a lower value means a higher priority, and the number of levels is left to operators.
sections.eli5: A new tag value says this is a shared spare road. A small number on it says who goes first, and the smallest number wins.

sections.title: Preemption and Shared Resource Notifications
sections.content:
The SMP preemption priority is used by the APS protocol to resolve competition for shared resources. The Setup and Holding priorities in SESSION_ATTRIBUTE are not used for this, which avoids a complex policy. Intermediate nodes MUST store the priority from the Path message. A preempted LSP MUST NOT be terminated, and the end node MUST keep refreshing working and protecting LSPs regardless of failure or preemption.

When a lower-priority protecting LSP is preempted, the intermediate node MUST send a Notify message with error code "Notify Error" (25) and sub-code "Shared resources unavailable" (17) to its end nodes, which MUST stop using that LSP and try another protecting LSP. The same message is sent if shared resources fail.

When resources become available, a Notify with sub-code "Shared resources available" (18) MUST be sent, and recipients may reinitiate protection switching if they still need it.
sections.eli5: If a more important car takes the spare road, the others get a warning to stop. When the road frees up, they get another message saying they may try again.

sections.title: Security and APS Configuration
sections.content:
The security threats in RFC 4872 also apply. In addition, an attack on a link used by the primary LSP of a higher-priority LSP can disrupt a protecting LSP elsewhere. In the example, attacking link B-C could disrupt traffic on [H,E,F,G,K] if [A,E,F,G,D] has a higher priority. Detailed knowledge of topology, routes and priorities helps an attacker.

The APS channel between adjacent nodes is configured by means other than GMPLS signaling, before any protecting LSP is set up. APS message formats and identifiers are technology or vendor specific, so further APS configuration requirements are out of scope.
sections.eli5: Breaking one far-away road can quietly knock out someone else's spare, so keep the map and the priority list private.
